title: Australian dance audiences and the six o'clock drinking laws
summary: Audiences dance rather than listen, and bars close at six, so dance halls are dry, leaving the town full of drunks.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: Well, what does the public do when they listen, then?

They dance. They dance. They don't even listen. They dance. Um, most of them are, like most publics, uh, are not very interested at all. Mm-hm. They dance to it. Which is, uh, good, I think, from the playing point of view. You can just, uh, concentrate on your playing without having to, uh, feel that you've got to move, uh, an audience that's just sitting still in front of you by doing something, uh, spectacular. So do I.

Yeah. It's a pleasant change to hear a band like that again. Very rare that you get to hear that around New Orleans anymore. Mm-hm. Dance halls are pretty well gone. There's a couple left that are still going, the Harmony Inn and the Legends, but I don't know if the bands are any good. It's a new Legends, a cousin of the old family. Anyway, uh, do they allow drinking in the jazz clubs, or do you have bars, or is it like you doing at all? No, no, no. It's, uh, it's much worse. It's ridiculous.
Uh, at six o'clock, the bars close, 6 p.m. Mm-hm. And, uh, no drink is allowed to be consumed after that time anywhere, much less in dance halls.
Um, so that, uh, it's just got to be coffee and coke, I'm afraid.
